Stir pasta, chorizo, and pesto passive aggressively. Add pasta water as needed, until pesto and chorizo fat emulsifies.
Taste for salt and adjust with pasta water or pesto as needed
Cut heat, finish with a dab of (optional) butter, stir once more.
Plate and enjoy!
pinkslaw & chickpeas

I owe everything to the Internet Shaquille, my goat.⁠09

ingredients
can of chickpeas (200g)
quarter head of red cabbage
1 medium carrot or 2 small carrots
½ red onion
4 radishes I think
fresh green herbs of choice (I used dill and carrot leaves)
grateable cheese of choice (I used comté)
lime / lemon
olive oil
honey / sugar
instructions
Make slaw ahead of time by adding thinly sliced not-yet-pink vegetables to a container alongside the juice of an entire lime / lemon, a big pinch o’ salt, and a smaller pinch of sugar / squeeze of honey. Toss together and let sit in the fridge for at least an hour.
When ready to eat, rinse and drain chickpeas, add to a flat microwaveable plate, and microwave for ~5 minutes.
Meanwhile, preheat pan. Add a healthy dose of olive oil, and toss in freshly microwaved chickpeas. Add a pinch o’ salt and fry until golden or at desired crispiness. 
(optional) After cutting the heat, I also like to toss the chickpeas with some bouillon powder.
On the side, roughly chop herbs. 
Add ½ of now-indeed-pink slaw, chickpeas, and herbs to the bowl. Taste for salt / acidity levels, grate cheese on top.
Toss and enjoy!

Title: Welcome to our new bloggers!--introducing the baby bloggers of 2026
Author: Chris Peterson SM
Article Content:
After much deliberating over the ~100 blogger applications we received this summer, we are happy to introduce you to our new baby bloggers.

We hired 8 baby bloggers —  four first years, and four older-than-first-years —  because that is the number of ‘2027s we expect to see graduating (between senior year and MEngs), and we aim to have rough conservation and continuity of posters.

Their cartoon faces (drawn by our peerless kitty with a pencil Sam Xu on the comms team) are below.

The newest apprentices to the posting guild.

 

In order of top row to bottom, left to right:

Title: Return to Campus--x^n
Author: Victor D.
Article Content:
I don’t know how to feel. “How do you feel about your last FDOC⁠01 ?” Great question. It (graduation) doesn’t feel so imminent unless I psyche myself to believe so. I can barely surmise what my life will look or feel like in a month, so how am I supposed to locate this day in my life relative to an event in June? It’s too far. I think thinking about it worries me more than it excites me though. So I’ve chosen for it to be remote, distant, but every “I’m a 4th year senior” incants the inevitable end.

I can scarcely recall my life before college now that I think about it. I remember it conceptually—names, events, classes, places—but seldom does it evoke real emotion in the way that my recent memories do.

So I can lean on my experience graduating high school only to fall through it, a phantasmagorical mist without physicality, only image, an image that feels to belong to me as much as a story I watch on television—which is to say, it no longer belongs to me, it belongs to an otherperson me who I’m not quite sure when I broke from them, lost them, when they died.

So I’m trying to imagine the image of my impending graduation and really I can’t comprehend it. I recently read They Both Die at the End; I wonder about the major theme, carpe diem to the utmost everyday; no kicking the can down the road indefinitely until it’s too late; when death wielding scythe already claws at the door.

So then I think about seizing my days to the fullest and I encounter a library stretching beyond the clouds and into the depths of the Earth, a bookcase of what to me are essentially innumerable combinatorial books upon bookshelves and on an infinitesimal minority I may glean only their title spines, and in their pages when I leaf through another book coalesces in its place while my eyes adrift, and the library itself grows the more I pull from its shelves and read and pull and read…

More done, and less is the proportion complete. If I were to live as though I were to die at the end of each day, I’d be frozen in place as Matteo in They Both Die at the End, unable to leave his room, terrified by risk and choice and combinations thereof.

It’s really a gift to have an inexhaustible library to discover… but alas I won’t be able to do everything, as the more I do the more it feels as though I haven’t done anything. Anyways, rather than fixity in fear, I’m just doing what I want to do now without too much concern of that-which-I-want-to-do-but-don’t-have-time-to-do-now.

Although I can’t do everything, anything is something. So everyday I do progress and exercise something I like: reading, writing, music, studying, walking, playing soccer… none are commensurable, and so I’ll do what I enjoy—shun the Opportunity Cost Demon!

Title: I didn’t know a lot coming into MIT--why does it feel so embarrassing to learn
Author: Jessica Z.
Article Content:
One of the most embarrassing memories I have happened during a summer program in high school. We had an introductory class teaching us how to use LaTeX, a typesetting system that can be used to write scientific documents. I, however, did not know what the class was actually about and showed up with a notebook, pencil, and no laptop.

I veryyyyy quickly realized my mistake when everyone pulled out their laptop and started typing, but I was too embarrassed to say anything, so I just sat at my desk and pretended to look busy.⁠01 About ten minutes into the class, the TA walked over to me and jokingly said that since I clearly already knew how to use LaTeX, I could help some of the people around me.

So, instead of spending a few minutes embarrassed to admit to my TA that I didn’t know what LaTeX was so I didn’t bring my laptop, I spent an entire class period embarrassed that the TA probably thought I thought I was too smart to participate. While I wince a lot thinking about this encounter from over four years ago, it’s a pretty good representation of how I’ve historically dealt with embarrassment. I hate looking like I don’t know what I’m doing, even if it’s true, and I hate asking a question that I think I should know the answer to. I also hate the possibility that someone might think I’m incompetent, even if nothing they’ve done suggests that they believe that.

In general, I think embarrassment clouds a lot of my experiences. In high school, I honestly used to get most of my work done by scheduling check-ins with people because I knew I would be too embarrassed to show up empty-handed. It was definitely not sustainable, but for a while, it worked.

All that to say, I cannot think of a period of my life when I was more consistently embarrassed than my first two years of college. In the spirit of being vulnerable, here’s a few things I did my freshman year:

Emailed my first-year advisor to ask why I was double-booked for a class because I didn’t know that recitation was different from lectures
Dropped 6.100A⁠02 because I got a 3% on my first microquiz
Cried in front of my 5.111⁠03 TA after recitation because I failed my first exam, while the next recitation section filed into the classroom
Cried HAPPY tears over getting a C on my 5.12⁠04 final because that meant I didn’t have to retake it⁠05

I also didn’t magically figure everything out my sophomore year:

Started and finished more PSETs that I’d like to admit the day they were due
Pulled a few too many all-nighters for Ring Committee⁠06
Talked to my advisor about taking a semester off and teared up about three times during our meeting

Andddd even into my junior year, I felt like I was still finding ways to embarrass myself:

Butchered my first industry interview because I misread their job description. I thought their work focused on lead (as in, the material) not lead discovery (aka figuring out what drugs are leading contenders for further studies)
During a final-round interview, a company VP asked how I had heard about them and why I was interested in the company, which was probably my cue to say something thoughtful about their work. Instead, I blanked and told him I had seen their logo on a lot of backpacks while I was living in D.C.⁠07

I spent a lot of my first two years at MIT nervous. I was constantly worried about what or how other people seemed to be doing. I also spent a lot of time believing I was making wayyy more “mistakes” than everyone else around me. At some point, I kind of forgot the whole reason I was here was to learn. And learning can feel, unfortunately, kind of embarrassing at times.

If someone had told freshman-year me, “You’re here to learn! Don’t worry!” I probably would have felt an urge to scream at them. Obviously I was taking classes to learn. Now, though, on the brink of my senior year, I realize I didn’t quite understand how much learning required me to become comfortable with other people watching me not know things.

Before college, I never would have reached out to friends for academic help as readily or as casually⁠08 as I do now. I wouldn’t have swallowed my pride enough to repeatedly ask for help when I was three lectures behind or not even sure where to start on a PSET. I wouldn’t have been forced to decide what I actually wanted to devote my time to after realizing I couldn’t take every class or join every club I wanted to. There was absolutely no universe in which high-school me could have dropped a class and felt okay afterwards. I’m also infinitely more comfortable now telling my friends when I’m struggling or frustrated or sad. I’ve gotten better at not ruminating over every tiny “mistake” because I realized there’s no point in being embarrassed about trying to learn something new.

Sometimes I think about how my parents had to grow up so quickly, particularly immigrating to a new country and worrying about finances much more than I have ever had to. I’ve been given this four year period where I can, and I’m expected to, mess up in varying amounts of severity. My parents didn’t have four years carved out for learning more about themselves and the world around them, and they certainly didn’t have time to be embarrassed every time they didn’t know how to do something. I feel so lucky to be in a place where I’m meant to learn, even when every mistake or decision can feel impossibly heavy. 

The exams I failed felt catastrophic but don’t take up any of my mental space today. The awkward interviews and dropped classes are now stories and inside jokes with my friends. The reality is that everyone struggles with learning something here at MIT, even if it doesn’t feel that way. There will always be another thing I don’t know how to do, and I think I’ve finally become a little more okay with that.

To the frosh: you never really stop learning about yourself here, which means you might find yourself embarrassed more than once, and that’s okay! Ask the stupid question, go to office hours for what feels like the tenth time to ask the same question, drop the class if you need to, and tell your friends when you’re struggling. Most importantly, bring your laptop to any LaTeX workshops. And if you don’t, remember that it’s not the end of the world.

You don’t have to, and certainly don’t, know everything coming into MIT, and I really think that’s how you grow the most <3

Title: how to get from east campus to the student center--things are not as they seem
Author: Boheng C.
Article Content:
you don’t have to care
you don’t have to listen
you don’t have to read
you just have to notice

                                    — maya kaul, ‘19

you already know the fastest path, but you might not know all of them. and there’s so many cool things that you get to see if you don’t take the fastest one.

start by walking out the entrance to the dorm. 
enter building 66 through the doors on the east.
go down the stairwell into the basement.
walk forwards and down the ramp, down down down, and count the poppies lined along the wall, growing short medium tall

stop at the end of the hallway.
look to your right: a double door leading to a ramp, but the right door is propped open and doesn’t seem to be able to close. there’s a pipe jutting out of the ceiling which stops it from swinging shut. how odd.
look to your center: another double door, this time sealed shut with one lock and one handle.
look to your left.

there’s something there, isn’t there?
there’s something there which might help you enter new locations. look for it. look for it, on the ground, next to the elevators, in the long hallway; comb through the ceiling lights and doorframes and the vending machine. 
did you find it?
go back the way you came, back up the ramp, and continue past the stairwell.
go forward until the end of the hallway.
make a right turn.
walk until you find a water fountain and drink from it, perceive the bitter cold sharp water as it ebbs into your mouth, and notice the fountain of youth to your left, dried up and exhausted of its former life.

continue down the basement hallway until the first junction, and turn right there.
turn left again.
take a paper cup (you brought a paper cup, right?) and fill it up with hot chocolate at the vending machine, two dollars, and ponder your hot chocolate with foam in this unremembered corner of the stata center, five meters beneath the grandeur of an auditorium lecture hall, condemned to oblivion, for just two dollars.
was this place forgotten on purpose or by accident?
walk further along the corridor until you reach the door to a stairwell. enter it.
watch the outlines of dirt footprints on the walls as they meander towards the top.
go back out and go through the garage door nearby.
turn left then right into the loading docks without descending into the parking lot.
choose — choose between keyboards and desks and chairs and refrigerators with dark growths and cracked monitors leaking their blood of liquid crystal.

go down the stairs at the end. 
walk straight until you get to the car lane entering the parking lot.
turn right and left on the sidewalk until the door, then walk through until you get to an odd vending machine and read the sign:

go back, back through the loading docks silent basement vending machines fountain of youth, back and back until the south stairwell of building 26, and take it up to the first floor and smell the drunken scent of overripe bananas, imbibe the air, and realize that there’s a kettle and packets of hot chocolate in front of you, and that you didn’t have to pay two dollars at the basement vending machine earlier.

head into building 16 and up the short stairs to building 8.
just before reaching the infinite corridor, look up at the ceiling, past the network of dangling pipes. 
it reads GULLIBLE.
go forwards a bit and turn right, into the stairs down into the basement.
make a right and soon after a left until you get to what looks like an elevator.
is it an elevator?
walk back into the long corridor going west.
stop at the shelves full of old printers and books and manila folders and screws and cryptic circuit boards and pamphlets and water bottles.

turn right and walk until you reach building 13.
find a short door to the right of two vent openings. 
notice that the bottom vent has three of its four screws missing, while the top vent is intact.
continue forwards and turn left.
look up at the pipes suspended from the ceiling, contorting and wrapping and dancing around themselves.

go forwards through the hallway, notice behind you the surveillance camera mounted at eye level, bulbous shadowy lens watching through the cover.
go to the end of the hallway in building 9, before it makes a bend.
peer through the sliver between the double doors at the end of the hallway and look at the vastness on the other side, above and below, vast labyrinth of ducts and lights, and peer all the way until the end and maybe see a black rectangle on the wall adorned with white lettering, ornate flowing borders like the label of a bottle of bourbon.
turn the corner in the hallway and find the elevator.
go up the elevator to the ground floor and walk out the atrium of building 9.
run straight across massachusetts ave. because it’s already late, the street and its cars long asleep, the world powerless to stop you.
arrive at the front of the student center and join the cluster of other frosh already gathered there at 10 pm on this night,

new to the scene,
for now a little green.

Title: IHTFP (PE registration edition)--the T in MIT stands for sporT
Author: Janet G.
Article Content:
Claim: MIT is a sports school, not a tech school.

Proof: ⁠01 Since this claim is a two-part claim, [MIT is a sports school] AND [MIT is not a tech school], we will set about proving both parts.

Part 1: MIT is a sports school

I could go on and on about how MIT has an excellent athletics record: from the Admissions page alone, we have the largest NCAA Div III varsity program in the nation, we have over 470k square foot of recreational space, and we have the most Academic All-America citations out of any DIII school in the nation.

The blogs prove it too: I’m unfortunately not a jockblogger,⁠02 but our most recent jockblogging icon & queen Emiko P. ‘25 has written some MANY excellent blogs about her time as a varsity athlete, and Gloria Z. ‘26 and Kano T. ‘26 also wrote a great blog about gyms at MIT.

But even as your average chud at MIT who goes outside once in a blue moon and prefers to rot in bed over a morning run, I would like to contribute proof that MIT is a sporty school.

MIT has a rigorous PE requirement: if we want to graduate, we have to earn eight (8) PE points and meet the swim requirement by taking a swim class or passing the swim test. This generally means that you have to take 4 PE classes (though of course you are welcome to more if you wish) throughout your time at MIT, and you also have to know how to swim. Moreover, we have a fun little Pirate certificate, which certifies you as a pirate and helps you join the ranks of other notable pirates like Blackbeard, Ching Shih, and Matt Damon⁠03 .

I’ve taken some great PE classes in my time at MIT: I’ve done Archery, Air Rifle, and Weight Training, all of which were really fun and quite informative.

one of my first attempts at archery... i believe i was the green arrows so as you can see i did uh very interestingly
CAN YOU TELL I WAS SO PROUD OF THIS OEN
shoutout matt lavita my rifle instructor goat bro was so chill
he even put us in his intro slideshow for future rifle sessions LOL
weight training was also really cool because we got to go to the newly renovated special varsity-athletes-only training gym for this pe class (which was indeed rlly nice)

You can’t really go wrong with PE classes at MIT. The worst they can be are just chunks of mandatory study breaks where you can’t think about classes, but exercise in general is just really fun. People mostly don’t take them for two reasons: being too hosed to fit anything into their schedules, and a secret second reason I’ll elaborate on soon.

Part 2: MIT is NOT a tech school

Look. As much as I love this school, as much as we have groundbreaking research and engineering every other day, the tech at this school kinda SUCKS. Why do we still have janky physical keys for accessing all our dorms? Why do the doors at Lobby 7 swing so erratically and activate at a questionable frequency?⁠04 Why does the print service at this school have file size limits for uploading? Why does the wifi spazz out every other day or so??

I’m not spiteful enough nor nerd enough to answer these questions, but they haunt me every day. There’s a running joke about MIT: we build frontier technologies, only for export.

Anyway, to bring these claims together in an effective case study, I bring you:

~ ✨ Janet gets screwed over by PE Registration✨ ~

PE Registration happens at 8am. It happens three times in the Fall semester (two for each of Q1 and Q2, one for IAP⁠05 ) and twice in Spring, which is oftentimes the only reason why many folks (myself included) will bother to get up anytime remotely around 7:45am.

People usually notify their friends and family for the occasion and celebrate / commiserate depending on the outcomes of the PE registration roulette.

the dedication to PE registration means that u wake up whenever PE reg is happening... even if it's 5am in the morning...

Anyway, this time it was no different. Since I’m an ailing senior with terrible time management skills, I still need to take one more PE class⁠06 to graduate.

uh oh

Since it’s such a big deal, and I did want a good PE to round off my experience, I actually moved a flight I had scheduled at 6am in order to ensure that I could register for PE at 8am.

Rule one of PE registration is that you always pre-plan what you want and go for Quick Registration on the website, because you gotta MOVE FAST. The most popular spots (mostly just the Pirate Certificate sports, along with some that are rare and interesting eg. Pilates) will fill up in an instant, so you better optimise whatever you can.

I decided to be ambitious and try for fencing, which is always one of the most difficult: it’s a Pirate certificate sport, there’s often only 1-2 classes, and the class sizes are small. Not sure why I did that because I haven’t gone through the war of PE registration in the last full year. Hubris…

the way to read the number columns is, from left to right: remaining open spots (0, obviously), number of people on waitlist, and capacity. you can see that archery has a capacity of 98 people, pistol + rifle has a capacity of 60, sailing has a capacity of 90, and fencing has a mere 32… sob

Rule two of PE registration is that you always have multiple tabs open. And multiple browsers open. In fact, get a second laptop if you can (I’m mostly joking). This is how I ended up looking crazy locked in at the airport at 7:59am in the morning.

I’M READY CAP’N

This year, I decided to be a little scientific and had one laptop on the airport wifi, and the other laptop on my hotspot. The internet speed test results said that it was okay, so I was counting down to refresh the page in time for 8am sharp.

i’m sooo ready….

Rule three of PE registration is that the site WILL crash, and crash badly. When too many clients request the same server, the server will go down. Unfortunately, the tragedy of the commons exist, so you just gotta spam requests yourself aswell.

Title: All the 2026 i3 videos megapost--see the dorms!
Author: Aiden H.
Article Content:
MIT likes to be unique in many ways: majors are called courses, everything from classes to buildings are numbered, and maybe more unexpectedly, MIT has a very unique dorm set-up. Dorms are not filtered by class year, there are no special “honors” dorms, and no dorm is meant to be “nicer” or an “upgrade” to others.⁠01

The biggest distinguishing factor between MIT dorms is each’s tight-knit and well-defined community. Undergrads take part in multiple campus-wide dorm exploratory events⁠02 to understand each dorm’s culture and where they want to live.

In order to help with this decision process, dorms make/compile Interactive Introduction to the Institute (I3) videos for students to explore the dorms and their culture each year. These are posted under each dorm on MIT’s Housing and Residential Services website. 

The following, in alphabetical order by dorm, are all the of 2026 i3 videos embedded for easier access. Take a look!

Note that New House has its 6 floors submit their own i3 videos, all of which you can access here separately. Simmons did not submit a 2026 i3 video, but last year’s is available here.

Title: i went to the ig nobels!--(last year) (there is also a vlog)
Author: Ellie F.
Article Content:
It’s funny how optimistic summer makes me. Every August, I sign up for more classes than ever and dream about the clubs I’ll join and the adventures I’ll have over in Cloud Cuckoo Campus, where psets are fun and get done in a reasonable amount of time and I never have to sacrifice anything, ever. It’s falling in love with someone you see once a year–highly unrealistic, I suppose, but can you help it? Isn’t it fun?

All this to say I thought I was some hot stuff going into last fall, and it ended in a nontrivial amount of tears. But before it ended, I’d made up my mind to shoot my shot with the Ig Nobel Prize and either ask, guilt trip, or plead my way into a press pass. This was much easier than I had anticipated.

I went to the ceremony and had a life changing experience, et cetera and so on, and I left with about an hour of footage. I’d make a vlog, and it would be fun, and I’d be done in a month or so, and then maybe I’d make a room tour because my roommate and I finally put up decorations after throwing the idea around for all of freshman year.

The fall semester ended (I didn’t edit). I went home for winter break (I didn’t edit). I came back to campus for all of IAP (did not edit). I had no plans for all of spring break (can you see the pattern yet). So that leaves the summer.

I moved into a two bed one bath house in California and bought groceries and new shoes from the shopping center three pedestrian crossings away. I hung up my shirts in a color gradient and learned which drawers in the kitchen didn’t slide out quite right. And when I was settled in, I was resolved that this time, really, I would edit the vlog.

My summer ended up being the Caltrain on more evenings than not, crowding myself in with the Giants fans in orange and young urban professionals leaving the office but still working on the way home. I’ll tell you about it more another day. But my summer certainly wasn’t Adobe Premiere.

My new mantra was to do it when I got home, to Arkansas. That’s where my excuses ran out. I’d sit down at my computer each evening, meaning to watch through my interviews and write a script. I had nothing else to do, after all. Instead, I ended up at the piano, relearning old songs and the feeling of the stretch in my hands.

It’s awful that only a hard deadline could make me finish this project. Honestly, I don’t like what that says about me. I’m hoping that it’s not an unchangeable fact, and I’m hoping that this is the semester where I change it, but then I look at my classes and despair just a little.

The fall equinox isn’t for another few weeks, and I’m dreaming again. I can’t help myself, and, well, it’s really, terribly fun.

Title: i did nothing these past two years, part 1--starting over?
Author: Boheng C.
Article Content:
this morning, i got kicked out of my lab.

of course, it felt like a surprise when i heard for the first time. it was a surprise. had it not been just weeks before when i trod headfirst into that office, illuminated by the hot summertime glow of killian court, a bit suffocating in its boisterous proclamations of lemonade encased in sweat and retreat to air-conditioned dorms, and had i not declared bright-eyed to my postdoc supervisor that i wanted to continue this research for another semester? and had he not said yes, yes of course? and in that moment, had i not felt that i was meant to be there? that i belonged? that i, after all, was truly there?

or had those few weeks grown monstrously into months already, and had that hot summertime glow been instead the soft vernal midday sun, and had the buds of spring barely emerged from their snowy blanket?

what have i been doing all these months?

what have i been doing for two years?

 

the research was fun. i loved it even, i loved continuum mechanics and calculus of variations and i loved making all the plots and doing fourier transforms. i loved being able to work on the research wherever i wanted. i loved watching terms cancel out and variables dance around the page. in short, it was everything that i could’ve asked for in a urop⁠01 . of course, it was a bit abstract, and sometimes difficult to see how the assumptions translated into physicality, but i felt like i was doing something.

and yet, i can only ask why i spent so little time on the research. certainly, i was busy and i had less time than i wished that was left over for the urop. but time and time again, when faced with the choice to do something i dearly enjoyed, i said no.

and so, this morning, when i declared bright-eyed to my pi⁠02  that i wanted to continue this research for another semester: “i think not.”

Title: A Recipe for Staying Whimsical--and dealing with stress in the upcoming months
Author: Richard O.
Article Content:
With the “-ber” months right around the corner, it’s very easy to get caught up in things like schoolwork, college applications, exams, projects, and other stressful activities that make it hard for you to make time for yourself. But in order to make sure you don’t burn yourself out, it’s sometimes helpful to set aside an hour or two where you step away from everything and take time to enjoy some of the small things you love, because the most important part of life is experiencing and not staring at a computer screen or assignments for hours on end with no breaks. So today I decided to whip up a recipe for staying whimsical that you can bake on your own anytime you’re hungry for a break.

Ingredients:
1 quart of an optimistic mindset
5 tablespoons of your favorite songs
1 bowl (or two) of your favorite snacks or a pint of ice cream
3 cups of positive affirmations
3 tbsp of your proudest memories or moments
A close app feature on on all social media services and online assignments
1/2 cup of a friend or family member you can talk to
1 version of you that will figure things out
2 mixing bowls
A spatula/whisk
A chopping board
An oven (though a room, library, or sidewalk with ample sunlight is preferred as a substitute)
Plastic wrap
A baking pan
Instructions:

Step 1. Dissociate from expectations:

To get started, take the version of you that will figure things out and separate all expectations for yourself on the chopping board.
Move the excess expectations aside
Place the remaining version of you in a mixing bowl and pour in the quart of an optimistic mindset. 

 

Step 2. Relax:

Allow the bowl containing you and the optimistic mindset to rest for 15 mins. 
In your second mixing bowl, add the following dry ingredients: 
5 tablespoons of your favorite songs
1 bowl or two of your favorite snacks or a cup of ice cream
3 cups of positive affirmations
Mix until satisfied.
Pour the dry ingredients into the bowl containing you and the optimistic mindset
Mix until all the ingredients are blended together
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and allow to rest and rise for at least 1 hour

 

Step 3. Prep the Oven/Substitutes 

If using an oven, check to make sure your oven is turned off (unless your favorite snack actually requires you to bake something and they’re still baking)
If you didn’t acquire the preferred substitutes to the oven, you now need to acquire them
Preheat the substitutes to a temperature associated with a decent amount of sunlight in the location of your choice
If frequent sunlight is unavailable, a room with windows will suffice

 

Step 4. More Mixing and Baking

Take your mixing bowl of primary ingredients and remove the plastic wrap
Sprinkle in the 3 tbsp of your proudest memories or moments and fold into the mixture
Pour the mixture into a baking pan
Lightly coat the mixture with the close app feature on on all social media services and school assignments
Place the baking pan in the preheated substitute and set another 1 hour timer.
While waiting, you can optionally put the 1/2 cup of a friend or family member you can talk to on a pan on medium heat and let simmer for at least 20 mins to add to the garnish
After 1hr, check to see if the items are ready to be removed
If not check back every 20 minutes until the texture is soft, fluffy, and ready to come out of its oven of choice

 

Step 5. Garnish and Enjoy

Finally, remove the pan from the oven and let cool for 15 minutes
On the chopping board take the leftover expectations from before and cut them into finely sliced goals and toss out any parts of the expectations that would spoil the final product or don’t seem to look appetizing. 
If you used the friend or family member you can talk to in this recipe, add the sliced goals in the same pan and mix them together.
Coat the cooled off version of yourself with the garnish and enjoy!

Title: last week, i failed at a jigsaw puzzle and knot theory--and some fears about returning
Author: Aiden H.
Article Content:
This past week, I made the mistake of trying to have a Sunday morning brunch, no reservation. After driving 20 minutes to the best brunch place around with my mom, sister, and girlfriend, none of us were surprised to learn we would have to wait at minimum another 20 before being sat.

And so began the saga.

To kill the time we rounded the corner to a cutesy puzzle and games store. After messing around with Lego flowers, Calico critters, and petting the live bunny they have randomly hanging around, I stumbled upon this beauty:

Priced at a relatively cheap $25, I thought a 1000 piece puzzle might be a little bit of a stretch considering I was leaving Colorado and heading back to MIT at 5 AM Wednesday morning but bought it anyway. Besides, at the point that you’re doing a puzzle, how much of a difference is 500 versus 1000 pieces? Also it’s a pretty distinctive and bright puzzle, so the pieces should be pretty easy to delineate.

Wrong.

I have a bad history with jigsaw puzzles. I always turn to them in a time of productivity crisis (see: COVID lockdown and summer breaks) when I feel bad if I just rot on my phone all day, but I don’t necessarily want to do actually productive work. A similar feeling is reached by reading excessive amounts or tracking my steps.

So what came upon me to believe that my girlfriend and I could crank out a 1000 piece puzzle in 48 hours? Narcissism and amnesia.

We started the first day strong enough, cranking out the edges in 1.5 New Girl episodes/45 minutes. Then disaster hit. I made the awful suggestion of starting at the bottom because the flowers were more distinctive than the mass of yellow above. A whopping six hours into the puzzle, we had only gotten this far:

The next day was much of the same, spending hours upon hours trying to speed run this god-forsaken puzzle, only to be here upon midnight:

With less than 24 hours left before my flight to Boston, we gave up on the puzzle.

***

My return to campus was as normal as ever. I picked up all of my summer storage boxes and said hi to friends as I made my way down the hall to my room, only to be faced with puzzle number two: untangling my fairy lights.

Like anyone under 30 with questionable taste, I have fairy string lights hung up around my dorm room to offset the harsh Walmart-brand overhead lighting that graces MIT dorms. Amongst the rush of packing and simultaneously half-passing my finals in the spring, my past self decided the best decision at the time was to rip-them-off-the-wall-and-shove-them-into-a-box-as-fast-as-possible, which admittedly did not help present-day Aiden when trying to untangle said lights.

I sat on my floor for genuinely an hour and a half trying both possible forms of detangling (trying to methodologically follow each strand and untangle one by one, and flailing it around until it miraculously untangles), of which neither were successful.

Sitting there angry and sweating, I noticed that my tangle of fairy lights looks a lot like a mathematical knot (and I guess a literal one), which is something I know nothing about but have always been interested in. So after 30 minutes of intense Wikipedia-ing and watching simplified YouTube videos, I learned my first fact about knot theory: unknotting numbers. Apparently the unknotting number is the minimum number of moves⁠01 it takes to turn a knot into an unknot, which is just math-ese for circle.⁠02 I also learned/AI-overviewed some constraints, learning that the unknotting number of any knots is always less than half the knot’s crossing number.

But wait wait wait, as learning too much would ruin my night and prove me a dumbass once again. Technically in math a knot must be “closed” so that all the end are connected, which is,  in all fair, completely ridiculous. Shoelaces? Not a knot. Rope? Not a knot. Ribbons? Not a knot. A circle? Definitely a knot but again not because it’s an unknot. (side note but Dr. Seuss would love knot theory).

My fairy lights? Not a knot.

Looking at my fairy lights again, I felt equally as stuck and now also bad at math. But knot or not,⁠03 I became convinced by their complexity to have at least a not-a-(un)knotting number of at least 74.

I sat down, analyzed it from all sides like those Rubiks cube guys, and pulled one string from the middle. I kid you not, in the most this-whole-thing-was-scripted way, the entire thing of lights came undone across my lap and was able to string out perfectly across my floor.

It turns out it had an “unknotting” number of 1. Like always, I made everything too complicated.

But look at that, I solved a puzzle.

***

In a very loose metaphor that is definitely not a stretch, I can’t help but feel like these experiences were premonitions on the coming semester.⁠04

Going into freshman year, I had the normal anxieties about moving to college. Most of these were social; will I have friends, like the dining halls, have enough personal space, etc. etc.? My concerns were solely about being able to survive and thrive in the lived experience of being at MIT. After a less-than-stellar freshman experience, I returned to sophomore year fearing things that I had felt become true: isolation, boredom, and stress at college.

Returning for a third time, though, I find that my nerves have been exacerbated but shifted. For the first time coming back, I feel not overwhelmed by the experinece of going to college, but my going to MIT. I feel unable to perform at a level that makes me feel confident–whether it be getting things done on time or literally being able to understand what is happening around me. I’m terrified of actual failure.

This is a pretty common sentiment at MIT. Call it imposter syndrome or whatever, but actually having a taste for MIT makes me feel less like an imposter and more like someone who just can’t handle it all again. I’m not anxiously dreaming up a difficulty in workload, I know it exists.

This is also not a common sentiment at MIT. Most people come to MIT and have an adjustment period where they learn school can be actually hard, but they get over this feeling as time goes on, and eventually as an upperclassman it just feels like school and not battling a dragon. I feel like I’m Benjamin Button-ing through these emotions. Freshman year academics? Totally fine and I would encourage you not to be stressed. Junior year? I’d shit my pants.

But then again everything is always a happy-ish medium. I will almost definitely be stressed this semester. I will also not experience anything I haven’t survived before. Everything will be manageable, I just need to find a way to manage myself going into it.

I guess only time will tell?

Title: Airport Problems, Three Years Later--we all have different coping mechanisms for coming back to school
Author: Janet G.
Article Content:
Good morning world! It is Sunday August 30, 4:48AM, which is morning enough. I landed from my Un*ted flight coming from San Francisco 5 hours ago. I am sitting on my mattress in Burton-Conner,⁠01 and my brain has no intention to sleep, which is how we’ve ended up here.

Unfortunately, this is not the first time I’ve ended up in a situation like this. In fact, it’s a very full circle moment for me: three years ago, I was also wide awake on my mattress in BC, fresh off a Uni*ed flight from San Francisco, questioning all the decisions that led me to this point of my life.

What happened the first time?

Okay quick speed recap. By one reason or another, my prefrosh self had comically terrible luck with flights: that summer I took ~10 flights, and all of them were either delayed, cancelled, or both. (It’s either that or U*ited is a terrible airline, but of course both can be true). I like to think that it was nominative determinism implicitive egotism (???) that they really said the Kiwi⁠02 should NOT be permitted to fly in any form. or at least have a really hard time about it.

Anyway, this time it was no different. I was flying from my summer program to go to Boston to start school, and a picture is worth a thousand words, so you can just see for yourself:

*deep breath* allllllright. little did janet at the time know that this was only the beginning... she thought she'd paid her dues with one (1) big flight issue...
can we talk about how out of ALL of these flights. i get it burbank is some random place #sorrynotsorry. but WHY IS BOSTON ALSO CANCELLED???
oooooooookayyyy deep breath janet deep breath

*hyperventilates harder* sorry my lungs are experiencing a technical issue
ah yes thank you u*ited for being factually accurate that you were in fact 10 minutes later than your LAST scheduled time

As you can see, I landed bright and early into Boston at the prime time of 11:48pm that day. To add insult to injury, they lost my baggage and somehow it ended up on another flight, so I literally had nothing aside from my carry on and backpack, and given that you know, Boston is notorious for being a city that never sleeps, and everything was closed, I couldn’t even buy bedding. My international student mentors Pranjal ‘26 and Mohit ‘26 very kindly decided to come to the airport and emotionally support me anyway, which was necessary because I don’t think there was any other way in which I would have navigated the MBTA while being deeply distraught. I also arrived earlier than basically all the other frosh and upperclassmen on campus because I was an international, and so I genuinely just had nothing else to do and no one to crash with. As such, in typical frosh energy, I asked the one Boston friend I knew whether he would drive around Boston with me and we would pull an all-nighter for funsies (because once again, no bed for rest anyway).

Anyway it was great. We got McDonalds, ate it by the water, drove around some more, came back, and then watched the sunrise over the bridge. I eventually got my luggage back and thus acquired my bedding two days later.

Ok so you’re like, what could have happened this time?

It’s literally all my fault. I forgot that I packed all my bedding into the storage pod that I’d rented out with a few friends for the summer, and I didn’t think about it until I like, landed in Boston at 11pm today. Also my luggage got delayed AGAIN (i swear, United, I Swear) and so I once again left the airport around the beautiful prime time of 12:30am. Except this time I took an Uber because I am an #employedwoman with #disposableincome.

I don’t even know what to say: I actually originally booked a red eye so I would land in the city and you know, maybe had time to go to Target to buy emergency supplies or something, but for some reason (I wanted to attend a friend’s masquerade gala, yes i know it’s literally all my fault) I rescheduled my flight to land at 11pm. BY MY OWN VOLITION. think about the consequences of your action before you change your flights kids

little did i know...
you know what. thanks united for being early for once. at least this helps make it clear that it was actually just 100% on me this time

It’s chill though. I ordered my favourite late night Chinese takeout this time instead and yapped with another friend since we are both back pretty early. At this point I’m on track to watching the sun rise over the bridge (again), and as a bonus I even have most of my luggage! 💀

Ok so why am I talking about this?

I have nothing else to do, like what do you expect me to do, sleep on this plain mattress? Sorry my bones are old and I have been spoiled by Real Bed™ with Cotton Sheets and Real Pillows

So in a comical twist of fate, my old bones did in fact fall asleep because the only thing worse than not having a Real Bed is not getting enough sleep after a few days running around packing and doing handoff stuff at work. No sunrise for me⁠03 RIP

But jokes about being old aside, it did feel pretty uncanny to be reminded of how much time had passed between then and now. I was no longer surprised by the wall of humidity when I got off the plane. I ran into luggage issues again and knew that it would be okay because I was tracking the airtags on my luggage. I have the disposable income to call an uber without feeling bad about it. I ordered my favourite Chinese takeout rather than McDonalds because I know better now. I’m a senior coming home, rather than an anxious freshman asking my mentors how they like the weather and what they’ve heard about BC floor culture.

I spent my entire summer working in San Francisco. People have been asking, how did you find it? and I’ve not been able to say anything more than it was a lot. I worked on contracts involving millions of dollars, changed jobs halfway through summer, and used up seventy polaroids for all the friends who visited my loft. I lived the 996. I went to dinners and socials and networking events every single night for weeks on end. I saw what life could be like post MIT, and I saw all of my SF-based friends settled and growing in a way that I had never quite seen myself. I was a rising college senior, and they were all working adults, many of them my age or younger yet much more weathered in years of experience in the Real World. I felt young, fresh, and naive.

It was hard to leave; it was easy to get sucked into the rush of it all. Everyone was doing such important work that would change the world, that had millions of dollars attached to them and even more. The work I was doing was glamorous or at least attached to glamorous causes, and I’ll be damned if I don’t admit that I loved it because it was so grand, so sexy. San Francisco had causes worth believing in and I’d loved it.

And yet, and yet—

I’m back in Boston now. I’m here on campus in my floor shirt, greeting fresh faces, hugging old friends. I ran my gameshow REX event ⁠04 and was met with a lot of enthusiasm in all their ayes and nyes, unsuspecting frosh victims falling into all the right jokes as they spelt the wrong words, and roasts and impressive displays of knowledge that I didn’t even expect. ⁠05 I walked to Next Dining with Conner 2⁠06 and Luna and Katelyn got stuck in line at Hibachi as everyone who tries to get Hibachi at Next always do, because it’s just that good. I came back from dinner to take a nap on my Twin XL mattress with a sheet and pillow that I stole from Phoenix, which happened after an hour long yap session where I lounged in his hammock and we gossiped about classes. I hung around the B1ners⁠07 at their destroy-the-wall event to snipe Veronica, but also to cheer on the frosh breaking the wall and to talk about which watermelons are the best watermelons. I feel old, a little tired, and all too familiar with this campus and its cobbled pieces of red brick, marbled columns, and brutalist concrete.

I love to linger. In San Francisco, everyone always has somewhere to be, and the only place that makes sense to linger at is work when you have a deadline to hit. Here in Boston, we’re not in a rush; none of us really have anywhere to be—at least not yet—and we all linger around, chatting about where we’re from, what we do, and the uncertainty of where we are going to next.

It’s good to be back.

Title: Just Released: Report of MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use--reacting to the report on AI and our education
Author: Chris Peterson SM
Article Content:
In January, MIT launched the Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training.

Today, President Kornbluth announced the final report of the committee. I have been spending my morning reading (and listening) to it, and I think it is one of the most important reports about MIT and its education in many years.

In her announcement, President Kornbluth wrote:

As the report makes clear, MIT was founded to help human beings develop their own powers of discovery, problem solving, and invention. That is still and will always be our essential work.

Against that backdrop, AI presents itself to us as a kind of superpower, with both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks. Our challenge now is to derive its benefits and counteract its harms, as we strive “to define and foster the highest-quality residential education – of humans, by humans, in support of human flourishing, and for the betterment of humankind.”

…But far and away the most important work will be cultural. As a community, we need to arrive at a shared understanding of the proper role of AI in education at MIT and in our life together on campus, along with shared norms and values around what we can properly do with these new tools, and what we should expect from and owe to one another.

MIT has deep ties to the birth and development of AI and – through our researchers and our graduates – to its future evolution. We therefore have a duty to prepare our students to know when and how to use AI effectively, wisely, ethically, and responsibly, and when not to use it at all. And we need to equip them to apply these formative personal lessons in whatever work they choose to do in the world.

…MIT is and must always be a place that activates the human mind and spirit and that unites creative people in fulfilling the Institute’s great mission. As we define the Institute’s next chapter, AI will test our commitment to that educational ideal. For the sake of our students, for the future of MIT and for the shape of our sector and our society, it’s imperative that we get this right.

I encourage anyone interested in MIT and our education to read it —  whether you are a prospective student/parent, an alum, or an teacher here or elsewhere. It shows the best of MIT’s reports: thoughtful, deliberative, and deep, rooted in institutional history while looking forward to the world as we find it.

I haven’t blogged much about AI, not because I don’t have thoughts, but because I haven’t been sure what to say. The technology has been changing rapidly. Many MIT alumni —  people I personally know, in some cases since they were in high school —  are involved on all conceivable sides of the debate and at every level of the sociotechnical stack. I’ve experimented with student AI use —  and student AI prohibition —  in my teaching in CMS/W. We’ve committed to not using generative AI on the blogs, and we have no plans to adopt it⁠01 in other parts of our admissions reading or selection apparatus. At the same time, I have used LLMs to help me with orphaned coding projects,⁠02 or to find typos or informational inconsistencies across 20+ years of posts.

In many blog posts over the years, I (and others) have talked about the idea of following compasses over maps in conditions of uncertainty. When you don’t know the destination or the route, you have to steer by fixed points: the principles and philosophies that are important to you as an individual and as an institution.

I am grateful that today President Kornbluth, and this report, articulated some of those fixed points on behalf of MIT: that the Institute exists “of humans, by humans, in support of human flourishing, and for the betterment of humankind.”

In the comments below, I’ll share some of my favorite excerpts from the report as I work through it, and I invite any readers to join me in the exercise. Together, in community, we can make meaning together, pointing towards the star we collectively pursue amidst the gathering clouds.

Title: two homes--a draft from three years ago <3
Author: Veronica P.
Article Content:
Yesterday, I went thrifting.

When I thrift, I am a girl on a mission. With far too many options and far too little gems, I must be swift and decisive, methodically and quickly moving my way down the racks, pushing hanger after hanger, making split second judgment after judgment.

But yesterday, something gave me pause.

It was a polo: pretty standard, visibly not my size, and (to be frank) kinda ugly. But there, on the breast, was the logo of my old catholic preschool- the place I’d learned my months of the year and animal sounds and how to spell my name.

Though amused, I moved on, but once I’d noticed it, I couldn’t quite shake it. In blue- the gym uniform I donned each day in my middle school locker room. In green- the sweat-wicking shirts of the local running club I’d spot on early mornings. In yellow- the high school baseball shirts worn by the team every game day.

Suddenly, I realized how much I’d taken for granted constantly being surrounded by semblances of home, by remnants of memories.

I can do what I can. I can lay out in my hammock and soak in the Houston heat till I’m sunburnt and sticky with sweat. I can drive down my neighborhood streets a million times a day and memorize every yard sign, count the high school parking lot stickers adorned on the cars passing by. I can fill my lungs up to capacity with the smell of my best friend’s house, till there’s no room left for me to laugh or scream or cry. I can stuff myself full of my mom’s chicken, the one she’d made just because she knew it was my favorite, even when she wasn’t planning on cooking at all.

I can see her trying too- staring at me a second too long across the kitchen table, squeezing me a bit tighter than normal, visiting my room more often for no particular reason at all.

It’s how you cope when you know things will never quite be the same; when you know that one can return to these people and these places, but they won’t be those same people or places you’d once known. My experience of MIT will send me back a different person, viewing familiarities with a newfound, unfamiliar perspective. Knowing this, I do my best to be mindful of every nuance and appreciative of every detail in these last months at home.

However, as I drive my car its final miles and read my last few books in that backyard hammock, I find myself seized by a sense of restlessness. I’m impatient to reach this next period in my life, that will be stressful and unfamiliar and busy and eventful. And the more I look around my home, the more I think “I love you, but wow, am I ready to leave you.” The muscles of my soul, longing for the opportunity to feel and fear and push, know they would otherwise atrophy. It’s remarkable, really, how these things come around right when you need them; that you can leave those objects of your heart before you grow resentful towards them, so that they can remain as such.

And, who knows. Maybe, in a few year’s time, I’ll flip through the racks of the thrift stores of Boston. I’ll see a shirt that reminds me of a memory far gone, pause, and smile.

What a joy it is to get to have two homes.

Title: i hate orthogonality--making my furniture diagonal
Author: Boheng C.
Article Content:
in a blog post a few months ago, i talked about my dorm last year (simmons hall) and its architectural eccentricities — its five thousand windows, its foreboding concrete walls, its twisty layout and cuboidal furniture and all its holes and colors.

this year, i moved to east campus, which had just finished remodeling. unlike last year, i know the names of everyone on my floor, which number around forty rather than fifteen. i get access to an elevator that reaches the first floor; i get a clean kitchen on my floor, a room to myself, a single big window with an opaque curtain rather than thirty-nine tiny windows with sheer transparent curtains. the lounges are filled with soft plushies and traffic signs and hair dye and strange cruft⁠01 that has been with our floor since time immemorial. my neighbors and i share similar thoughts about fire and opening strange doors.

but the dorm itself is painfully drab in comparison. the hallways are narrow and devoid of chalk drawings; the walls are disappointingly straight compared to the curves of simmons; the rooms are big rectilinear boxes instead of trapezoids and bends and semicircular arcs.

last august, after stepping off a sleepless five-hour flight and finding out that i had just become a second-year student⁠02 , i stepped into my room for the first time:

there was something wrong about this. it was all so immaculate and new; the walls were pale white and anemic and the floor was completely barren, even of dust, and the whole room had the intoxicating woody scent of new standard-issue furniture. absent were the unwieldy metal cube seats and bizarre shapes and the ghastly ceiling lights of simmons.

in a newly remodeled dorm that was more sterile than most hotels, i could only do one thing: i had to make my room weird, in spite of it all. and i did so, by rotating all of my furniture diagonally by fifteen degrees:

and there the furniture would remain, all the way until the end of the school year. living in a diagonal room was strange! here are some things i noticed about my self-inflicted skewness, in roughly chronological order:

my bed’s angle meant that there was now a thin triangular gap between its left side and the wall. unfortunately, my bed was also really high above the ground to fit the cabinets beneath it, meaning that i was perpetually afraid of rolling off into the corner for the first few nights. it got better after a while, when i realized that rolling off the other side was just as likely, but it was still a bit disconcerting to think of the foreboding cramped dark void that lay between my sleeping self and the wall.
even though it was so claustrophobic, the corner still offered limitless possibilities. would i use it for storage? as a space to stack old assignments and newspapers, to put circuits from electronic classes or piles of sweaters and jeans from years past? i ultimately settled on a thick cushion from my suitemates last year, on which i sat reading books every now and then, walled-in by bedframe and cabinets and closets on all sides. on some nights, when my psets felt interminable and the world grim and harsh, i would also retreat to the corner to cry and cry for a long time. after a while sitting there, encased by furniture so much taller than i was, huddled in noiseless half-darkness, sometimes, just maybe, things would get better again.

the drawers beneath my bed were originally positioned so that there would be a gap to their right, through which i could crawl under my bed to reach the corner. after a while, though, i found that simply hopping over the bed was easier.

there was an even smaller triangular corner between the closet and the wall less than ten centimeters wide at its widest point, which was only accessible through the bed corner and began to fill up with otherworldly conglomerations of dust and hair and pens that had fallen from the top of the closet. once or twice, i was scrolling my phone in bed and inadvertently let go and watched it tumble off the side into oblivion, at which point i had to push closet and bed away just to access the corner and brush off all the squalid grime from the screen. then i would feel a bit guilty and start wiping up the dust bunnies off the ground, but inevitably it would get just as dusty as before within two weeks.
over time, my bed would slowly try to drift back into alignment with the walls. i was never too sure why this happened, but i suspect that every time i hopped onto my bed or jumped off it or bumped into it while organizing my drawers below, there was always asymmetry in the force i would exert, which gradually but irrevocably rotated it. every week or so, i would have to manhandle my bed back into its original diagonality, lest a triangular gap emerge between the head of my bed and my closet. 
towards the end of the year, i grew lazy and let this gap fester insidiously, until i found that my pillow would sometimes start sliding and falling into the gap while i slept. one night it disappeared into the depths altogether. i awoke from my half-conscious state, startled by the sudden absence of softness beneath my head, and found to mild amusement and dismay that my pillow had simply vanished in the blink of an eye.
one of the main drawbacks of non-orthogonality was that the apparent size of the room shrunk dramatically. this was especially true considering my desk’s position as an island in the center of the room, which partitioned the very little space that was remaining into two narrow (diagonal) corridors. in order to have a comfortable space between my bed and desk, i had to push my desk back to the point where there was barely enough room for a chair, meaning that the back of the chair would constantly scrape the wall. the only solace was that only the right corner would ever hit the wall, since the chair, like everything else in this godforsaken room, was oriented diagonally.
one day, i was sitting at my desk and absorbed in a book. when i looked up from the book after a while, i found, to my mild consternation, that the walls of the room appeared to be slanted and my desk was straight, instead of the other way around. it only took a few moments for my spatial perception to recover, but it still frightened me a bit that the world could just rotate around me without warning. it did not help that the book i was reading was house of leaves.
the largest open space in the room was the quadrilateral region under the window that was bounded by the bed and desk. the first time one of my friends wanted to sleep over in my room, we had to endure several minutes of awkward experimentation in that space, growing more and more exasperated over the configuration of the cabinets and bed and the orientation of the shelves and eventually the diagonality of everything all at once, laughing at the fantastic absurdity of the situation, until we found that we could push one of the shelves further into the corner and relocate a moving box still towering with unused clothes and reroute the extension cable and have just enough space for blankets and a pillow and a sleeping bag — albeit at a 45-degree angle from the walls, stretching the entire distance between the far corner of the desk to the shelves.

during the winter, when i couldn’t open my window without having the floor freeze beneath it, i would prop open my door, and sometimes the cats on my floor would come in! kalashnikov, the gray tabby owned by my neighbor caleb p. ‘28, would run circles around my desk while i chased him and he would hop on my bed and leap atop my closet, dizzying height off the ground, and squeeze into the bedside corner and then the closet corner⁠03 , which was no wider than a hand and where he would hide in mischievous silence until i looked for him and he would dart out as if nothing happened.

all in all, did this result in a wide breadth of unnecessary inconvenience and turmoil in my life? of course it did. but did i also enjoy it? of course i did. i was more than prepared to sacrifice in the name of whimsy and mirth and deviance for the sake of deviance — whether it be a bit more time spent clearing dust in unfathomable locations or leaping over a bed to get to a corner or rotating my furniture back into non-orthogonality every few days or laying awake at night for a few minutes, slightly perturbed by the skew of the room around me, questioning what led to all this. it was all more than worth it in the end.

Title: Preparing for College--or not*
Author: Hala K.
Article Content:
As a pre-frosh, excited and stressed for my first year at MIT, I often looked to the blogs for advice. Every question I had seemed to have an answer, thanks to the sheer number of blogs out there and the diverse group of bloggers writing them – diverse in experiences, class years, majors, dorms, clubs, etc.

But there was one thing I couldn’t seem to find anyone writing about: how stressful the last few weeks before moving in for your first year are. The only group of students completely unrepresented on the blogs is pre-frosh, which means there is no one to write in real time about all the decisions you make and forms you fill out.

I was reminded of this last weekend when a close friend of mine from home was ranting to me about how worried she is about starting her first semester: “Should I take government or a writing seminar?” ⁠01 , “How easy is move in?”, and most importantly, “Am I the only one that feels like this?”

I remembered that about a year ago today, I actually wrote a blog about exactly this. So, if you’re feeling frustrated or worried, hear directly from pre-frosh Hala about her experience with it all:

I have a month two weeks until I leave for college. And while the average incoming freshman might tell you they’re stressed out about everything they still need to do – I’m not.

And that’s exactly the problem.

I do have a lot to do, I’m just not stressed about it. I’ve entered this emotional purgatory, where I’m fully aware that time is flying, and yet, I’m acting like I have years to prepare. It’s a special kind of self-delusion.

So I’m here to highlight all of the things I’ve yet to do and who knows, maybe writing this blog will finally drag me back to reality.

Let’s start with housing. I’ve recently received the ABSOLUTELY DEVASTATING⁠02 news that I’ve been placed in a triple. Only 2% of McCormick rooms are triples, so what are the chances I’d be that unlucky? Well… 2%, but you know what I mean.⁠03

Though aside from knowing the number of roommates I’ll have, I know almost nothing about my future home. What does the room look like? No clue. What size are the beds?⁠04 Couldn’t tell you. Do I need to bring my own trash can?⁠05 Probably, but I have yet to Google it.

What I do know is that I have big plans for my room: fairy lights, color coordination, Pinterest-board-level vibes.⁠06

Have I bought anything to meet that goal? You should know by now that the answer is no.

Though I have spent hours debating between two color schemes:

Blue and white (minimalist, peaceful, probably smells like the sea)
Or sage green and pink (artsy, cozy, definitely owns a record player even if I don’t)

At this rate, I’ll decide by the time I’m halfway moved in. Don’t we get a whole week⁠07 for that anyways?

Then there’s spending time with people at home before I leave. I keep saying I need to hang out with my friends – my best friends since childhood, people who know me better than anyone. But somehow, I keep choosing to stay home and dive into the next Throne of Glass book instead. 

I even try to blame it on not having a license, but then someone offers to pick me up or make plans… and I still hesitate.

I think it’s because every hangout now feels like a last. The last time we rap Hamilton in Noor’s car. The last time I watch Maryan down a Big Gulp. The last time we yell at Jana for trying to hit high notes she is definitely incapable of hitting. The last time we go to Oyaki Sushi and order way too much off the menu. The last time we live just two minutes apart.⁠08

So it’s not that I don’t want to see them, I do. The problem is how much more time I wish I had with them… and how bad I am at saying goodbye.

Finally, there’s the to-do list full of small but important things I keep putting off:

Buying new clothes (because my wardrobe is still stuck in 10th grade)
Applying for TSA PreCheck⁠09
Getting a required vaccine I may or may not have forgotten about

Every day, I think, “I’ll do it tomorrow.” But tomorrow shows up too quickly, and the cycle repeats. My Notes app is crammed with unopened reminders, and my calendar only looks free because I stopped updating it.

Though I’ve realized that all of this is not procrastination, it’s denial. I want to be ready and I should be ready… but some part of me keeps dragging my feet.

So yes, I’m frustrated. Not with the decor, the errands, or the people I haven’t seen yet, but with the part of me that’s clinging to the comfort of avoidance. 

Because once the duvet color is picked, the bags are packed, and the goodbyes are said – then it’s real.

Title: Talent is everywhere. Opportunity should be, too--A conversation with LIVE by Po-Shen Loh
Author: Nicole Cooper
Article Content:
Intro: I’ve had the chance to work with LIVE, developed by Po-Shen Loh, on expanding access to rigorous STEM learning for students in rural areas. Access to curriculum in rural and small-town communities is something I care deeply about, and in talking with their team, I quickly saw how much our missions overlap. So this is a joint blog post between LIVE and MIT Admissions, presented as a bit of a conversation so you can see some of the behind-the-scenes thinking happening at MIT and LIVE. 

LIVE: In many rural communities, students are just as capable, curious, and hardworking as anywhere else, but their opportunities are often limited by geography and resources. Access to advanced learning programs is uneven, meaning a student’s potential can be constrained by their zip code rather than their abilities. Yet these communities have something important: students who are motivated, independent, and deeply connected to the places they call home. When given the right opportunities, these students can thrive and lead in ways that benefit both themselves and their communities.


From our side: In our work in MIT Admissions, we meet students from rural communities every year who are doing extraordinary things with the resources available to them. What we see again and again is that talent is not limited by geography, but opportunity often is. That gap can show up in different ways: fewer advanced courses, limited access to enrichment programs, or simply not knowing what pathways are available. Expanding access is not about changing who is talented, it is about ensuring that more students have the chance to develop and demonstrate that talent.


LIVE: At the same time, traditional classrooms have to follow state standards in their math curriculum, which are important, but students also need chances to practice critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving. In rural schools, where access to enrichment programs can be limited, these experiences can be harder to come by. This is exactly the moment LIVE was created for: a program that brings hands-on, interactive learning directly to students, helping them develop real thinking skills, build confidence, and explore their full potential.
LIVE is designed to go beyond the classroom and help students develop inventive problem-solving skills. Over time, students gain a stronger understanding of math, but more importantly they develop skills that carry into other subjects and real-world situations. Furthermore, classes are designed to be highly engaging and dynamic. They run as interactive livestreams, where instructors are drawing, and teaching in real time. Students can jump in on mic or in a live chat overlay to ask questions. This imitates how students naturally engage with social media content today. As a result, students look forward to every class as they develop skills to make an impact in the communities they care about.


NICOLE: Experiences like these matter not just because they build academic skills, but because they change how students see themselves. We often hear on the road in rural areas from students who are unsure whether spaces like MIT are “for them,” especially if they come from schools where advanced coursework or STEM enrichment opportunities are limited. Programs like LIVE can play an important role in bridging that gap, helping students build confidence in their ability to engage with challenging material and to see themselves as part of a broader community of learners.


LIVE: One of the most unique parts about LIVE is our instructors, our LIVE Math Stars. They are high school and college students who are not only strong in math, but also professionally trained in communication, presentation, and even improv comedy. The goal is to develop people who are not only brilliant, but also confident, expressive, and genuinely kind to others. They learn how to connect with students, lead conversations, and create an engaging environment that feels welcoming and supportive. This challenges the stereotype that STEM students lack social skills and instead helps develop well-rounded, confident, kind leaders. Every instructor goes through a selective process to ensure they are kind and want to make a positive impact in the world. This is what sets us apart.


NICOLE: There is often a misconception that students from rural communities are somehow less prepared for rigorous academic environments. In reality, what we see in the admissions process is that many of these students have developed resilience, independence, and problem-solving skills in ways that are deeply aligned with what institutions like MIT value. Expanding access to opportunities like LIVE does not take anything away from other students, it simply allows more talented students to fully realize their potential.
This work is grounded in the philosophy of “thought+full,” developed by Professor Po-Shen Loh. It’s the idea that real success comes from combining deep care for people with thoughtful problem-solving skills. That philosophy shapes what they teach and how tjeu teach it. This philosophy resonates with how we think about education at MIT. We are not only looking for students who can solve problems, but students who care about the impact of those solutions and the communities they serve. That combination of curiosity, care, and collaboration is what drives innovation forward.


LIVE: For schools serving overlooked communities, we offer a meaningful partnership through the LIVE Math Scholarship Program. We prioritize partnering with schools in small towns or rural areas, as defined by the National Center for Education Statistics, as well as those where a majority of students are eligible for free or reduced lunch. The 6th grade students from our partner schools can be nominated by school leaders to apply to our LIVE Math Scholarship Program. Accepted students will be awarded full-tuition scholarships to our classes.At the same time, our paid classes are open to any student, helping us grow a diverse and connected learning community. As students progress, there are also opportunities to step into leadership. High school students can apply to become LIVE Math Stars, to teach and mentor middle school students, while building real experience in communication, teaching, and leadership.


NICOLE: For students reading this, especially those from rural or small-town communities, we want to be clear: you do not need to have access to every resource to be a strong applicant, and you do not need to wait until college to start exploring what you are capable of. Seeking out opportunities, whether through programs like LIVE or in your own community, is one way to begin building confidence in your abilities and expanding what feels possible.


LIVE: If this resonates with your school or your students, we’d love to connect. To become a LIVE Math Scholarship Partner, you can email scholarship@poshenloh.com. High school students interested in applying to be an instructor through our LIVE Math Stars program can get started here: https://live.poshenloh.com/jobs/star. More information about our classes and approach can also be found at https://live.poshenloh.com/.


NICOLE: We are excited about what is possible when more students have access to opportunities that challenge and support them. Broadening access does not narrow opportunity, it expands it and strengthens the entire community.

LIVE: We’re excited about the possibility of working together and creating meaningful opportunities for students.
